column1: Why is every astronomical observation necessarily a measurement of the past?
column2: Light propagates at finite speed c = 2.998×10^8 m/s, so received photons left their source earlier; e.g., Andromeda (d ≈ 770 kpc) is seen ≈2.5×10^6 years ago.

column1: What is the fundamental epistemic constraint that distinguishes astronomy from laboratory sciences?
column2: The observer cannot manipulate the system under study; all knowledge must be inferred from received radiation (plus gravitational waves and neutrinos), so the discipline relies on universal invariants and symmetry principles.

column1: State the inverse-square law relating luminosity L, distance d, and observed flux F, and identify what kind of invariant it is.
column2: F = L / (4πd²). It is a geometric invariant, exact in flat space and correctable in curved spacetime — the core bridge between intrinsic source properties and detector signal.

column1: Write the Planck function B_ν(T) and state the two thermodynamic laws derived from it.
column2: B_ν(T) = (2hν³/c²) · 1/(e^{hν/kT} − 1). It yields Stefan–Boltzmann total power per unit area σT⁴ and Wien's law ν_peak ∝ T, letting color directly infer stellar temperature.

column1: Why does blackbody radiation allow temperature inference independent of an object's chemical composition?
column2: Blackbody SEDs are thermodynamic invariants: any body in local thermodynamic equilibrium emits the same Planck spectrum at temperature T regardless of composition.

column1: Show how the two-body problem reduces to an equivalent one-body equation of motion.
column2: Define relative coordinate r = r₂ − r₁ and reduced mass μ = m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂); center-of-mass motion separates, leaving μr̈ = −(GμM/r³)r, i.e. r̈ = −(GM/r³)r with M = m₁+m₂.

column1: How many degrees of freedom in initial conditions define a unique Keplerian orbit, and what are they?
column2: Six: three initial position components and three initial velocity components. Each unique set maps to one unique Keplerian orbit.

column1: Derive why all Keplerian orbits are planar.
column2: Specific angular momentum h = r × ṙ is conserved: ḣ = r × r̈ = −(GM/r³)(r × r) = 0. Since h is constant, the orbit is confined to the plane perpendicular to h.

column1: What is the specific mechanical energy of an orbit, and what does its sign determine?
column2: ℰ = ½v² − GM/r is conserved (gravity is conservative). Sign of ℰ sets the orbit family: ℰ < 0 bound (elliptical), ℰ = 0 parabolic, ℰ > 0 unbound (hyperbolic).

column1: How does SNR scale in the photon-limited regime, and what is the underlying statistics?
column2: Photon arrivals follow Poisson statistics with variance σ² = N_phot, so SNR = √N_phot = √(Φ·A·t_exp) — SNR grows only as the square root of integration time or collected photons.

column1: Why do modern astronomical measurements often require more than classical error propagation?
column2: Systematic errors frequently dominate statistical uncertainties, noise is often non-Gaussian, and correlated error structures and instrumental effects can mimic real astrophysical signals — demanding full error-budget and noise power-spectrum characterization.

column1: What is the common misconception about small perturbations in nonlinear astrophysical systems?
column2: That a small perturbation always yields a proportionally small response. In nonlinear regimes, linear approximations break down near regime boundaries, requiring stability analysis and explicit boundary-condition treatment.
